body:
this is not a new behavior.  try this in 1.3, same error:

    s.query(Thing.id).options(noload("owner")).all()

the difference is that Query now processes all the options and everything at the end:  https://docs.sqlalchemy.org/en/14/changelog/migration_14.html#many-core-and-orm-statement-objects-now-perform-much-of-their-construction-and-validation-in-the-compile-phase

this behavior is critical for performance.

I don't have a way to "fix" this other than just to ignore all invalid loader options in all cases, which seems bad also.
the best we could do is add some kind of "don't warn for any options" flag if with_entities() is called, but that seems pretty hacky too.

An option/method to explicitly discard existing load options could be a less hacky option.... Anyway, in this particular case I managed to [just remove the option](https://github.com/indico/indico/commit/2b5d695e2c6fdc22d36b6b82c62e11c9e418c978) since it apparently wasn't needed anyway, but who knows what other cases may have the same problem...

well the bigger problem is the idea of "with_entities()" in the first place.   I want to make things simpler so that you just build a single query up front that's what you want rather than undoing state that was already created.

IMHO the nice thing of `with_entities()` is that you can have a util function that returns a query, and then use all the things it does, but query just some specific data in the end.

In my particular example where I encountered the bug: usually the function searches rooms matching various criteria and returns those rooms, but in some cases all I need is the ID and another column with generated data, so i'm using `with_entities()` to avoid getting all the other things I don't need.

IIRC you can use `load_only` for that.

At least I use `load_only` to specify which column to load, I think sqlalchemy will still always add the primary keys with `load_only`, not sure if `with_entities` is the same
well that gives you entities though, and those eagerload options if any will take effect.   it's more lightweight to load the column alone.

Oh I missed the part where only the column were loaded.

The documentation is not really clear about it.
To load tuples I usually just use a normal select as I would with a table even with mapped models. I guess in the end they would build the same thing

I can think of ways to make this work but they are all a little on the elaborate side.   The one that is least elaborate is to also store a "generation counter" on the query.    when the entities are changed (which is now the _raw_columns collection), we bump that number.   the loader options themselves would also need to be associated with a specific generation counter.   we detect the use case here by observing a mismatch in the generation and dont error in that case, but we still attempt to apply the options.
I noticed that the loaders in the example use the strings, that are deprecated. Would using the relationship help in this case?

at the moment the loader strategies are pretty aggressive about pointing out things that dont make sense.  this was in response to angry users who werent using the options correctly and were completely confused, since the options gave no feedback at all if they made no sense.


    s.query(Thing).options(noload(User.id)).all()

    sqlalchemy.exc.ArgumentError: Mapped attribute "User.id" does not apply to any of the 
    root entities in this query, e.g. mapped class Thing->things. Please specify the full path 
    from one of the root entities to the target attribute.

that error message was not an accident :)   i was trying to spell things out as clearly as possible.
so maybe we keep messages that have to do with entity mismatch as above.    but then "only column entitiies", which is a separate message, we can soften on that, maybe if they were after the fact.
oh or this, with_entities has only column entities, then we set disable eagerloads.  that might do it.   in any case we need to add a litle bit of checking when the _raw_columns is changed.
but it has to apply to Select.with_only_columns also

so this would do that, however it means we wont catch an error for something like this:

    s.query(Thing.id).options(noload("owner")).with_entities(Thing.id).all()

I'm a little nervous of behaviors that flip on and off at a distance like that.

issue.title: In 1.4, invalid SQL is generated when using `.with_entities` to get a `.join`ed model

labels.name: regression
labels.description: something worked and was broken by a change

labels.name: with_entities change
labels.description: issues related to the altered behvaior of Query w/ 1.4/2.0

issue.body:
If you query a model (e.g. with `session.query`) and filter on it, then join to a second model with `.join`, then use `.with_entities` to select that second model (the one you just joined to), SQLAlchemy will include the _second_ model in the `FROM` clause. This can cause issues later in the query. Version 1.3 did not include that second model in `FROM`.

## Example
If you run this code:

```python
import sqlalchemy as sa
from sqlalchemy.ext.declarative import declarative_base
from sqlalchemy.orm import sessionmaker

DeclarativeBase = declarative_base()
Session = sessionmaker()
session = Session()


class First(DeclarativeBase):
    __tablename__ = "first"

    pk = sa.Column(sa.Integer, primary_key=True)


class Mapper(DeclarativeBase):
    __tablename__ = "mapper"

    pk = sa.Column(sa.Integer, primary_key=True)
    first_pk = sa.Column(sa.Integer, sa.ForeignKey("first.pk"), nullable=False)
    second_pk = sa.Column(sa.Integer, sa.ForeignKey("second.pk"), nullable=False)


class Second(DeclarativeBase):
    __tablename__ = "second"

    pk = sa.Column(sa.Integer, primary_key=True)


query = session.query(First).filter(First.pk != 1).join(
    Mapper,
    Mapper.first_pk == First.pk,
).join(
    Second,
    Second.pk == Mapper.second_pk,
).with_entities(Second)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(query.statement)
```

You get an output of:

```sql
SELECT second.pk 
FROM first, second JOIN mapper ON mapper.first_pk = first.pk JOIN second ON second.pk = mapper.second_pk 
WHERE first.pk != :pk_1
```

This is invalid, as the first `JOIN` references the table in the first `FROM`. Running this query in Postgresql gives an error message like:

`invalid reference to FROM-clause entry for table "first" Hint: There is an entry for table "first", but it cannot be referenced from this part of the query.`

In SQLAlchemy 1.3.23 I get this perfectly valid SQL output instead:

```sql
SELECT second.pk 
FROM first JOIN mapper ON mapper.first_pk = first.pk JOIN second ON second.pk = mapper.second_pk 
WHERE first.pk != :pk_1
```

In my case I think I can pretty easily work around the issue by rewriting the query but I figured I should report it since a straight upgrade caused a test to fail 😅. Thanks!


**Versions.**
 - OS: macOS 11.3.1
 - Python: 3.8.9
 - SQLAlchemy: 1.4.15
 - Database: Postgres 10.12
 - DBAPI: psycopg2

body:
**Mike Bayer** has proposed a fix for this issue in the **master** branch:

**memoize current options and joins w with_entities/with_only_cols** https://gerrit.sqlalchemy.org/c/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/+/2871

as noted in the above gerrit and issue #6503, I took the elaborate approach which is that the "_options" and the "_joins" etc. are all stuffed into a brand new kind of object that is pushed onto a stack whenever with_entities() or with_only_columns() is called.   that new object then participates in all the caching, adaption, etc. and serves as the previous version of the query before the entities were changed.   then the joins/options are processed in terms of the entities they were made against.


it's a very high ratio of complexity added vs. API surface, but we're getting more consistent complaints about this one.

issue.body:
**Describe the bug**
Since version 1.4.19 (in particular commit https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/commit/5b3e887f46afdbee312d5efd2a14f7c9b7eeac65 fixing https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/issues/6503 and https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/issues/6253 ) the behavior when generating queries using union seems wrong. I'm not 100% sure it's because of the union, but this is the case I ran into. Version 1.4.18 worked fine.

**To Reproduce**
```py
import sqlalchemy as sa
from sqlalchemy.ext.declarative import declarative_base
from sqlalchemy.orm import relationship, sessionmaker

DeclarativeBase = declarative_base()
Session = sessionmaker()
session = Session()


class Parent(DeclarativeBase):
    __tablename__ = "parent"
    id = sa.Column(sa.Integer, primary_key=True)


class EventInvitation(DeclarativeBase):
    __tablename__ = "a"

    id = sa.Column(sa.Integer, primary_key=True)
    parent_id = sa.Column(sa.Integer, sa.ForeignKey("parent.id"))
    parent = relationship(Parent)


class EventResponse(DeclarativeBase):
    __tablename__ = "b"

    id = sa.Column(sa.Integer, primary_key=True)
    parent_id = sa.Column(sa.Integer, sa.ForeignKey("parent.id"))
    parent = relationship(Parent)


parent_id = 1
x = (
    session.query(EventInvitation)
    .filter(EventInvitation.parent_id == parent_id)
    .outerjoin(EventResponse, (EventResponse.parent_id == EventInvitation.parent_id))
    .with_entities(EventInvitation, EventResponse)
)
y = (
    session.query(EventResponse)
    .filter(EventResponse.parent_id == parent_id)
    .outerjoin(EventInvitation, (EventInvitation.parent_id == EventResponse.parent_id))
    .with_entities(EventInvitation, EventResponse)
)
print("UNION")
print(x.union(y))
print("UNION+COUNT (simulate x.union(y).count()")
print(x.union(y)._from_self(sa.sql.func.count(sa.sql.literal_column("*"))).enable_eagerloads(False))

```

**Output**
This is the correct output using 1.4.18:

```sql
# BEFORE, UNION
SELECT 
  anon_1.a_id AS anon_1_a_id, anon_1.a_parent_id AS anon_1_a_parent_id, anon_1.b_id AS anon_1_b_id, anon_1.b_parent_id AS anon_1_b_parent_id 
FROM 
  (
    SELECT 
      a.id AS a_id, a.parent_id AS a_parent_id, b.id AS b_id, b.parent_id AS b_parent_id 
    FROM  a
    LEFT OUTER JOIN b ON b.parent_id = a.parent_id 
    WHERE 
      a.parent_id = : parent_id_1 
    UNION 
    SELECT 
      a.id AS a_id, a.parent_id AS a_parent_id, b.id AS b_id, b.parent_id AS b_parent_id 
    FROM b 
      LEFT OUTER JOIN a ON a.parent_id = b.parent_id 
    WHERE 
      b.parent_id = : parent_id_2
  ) AS anon_1

# BEFORE, UNION+COUNT
SELECT 
  count(*) AS count_1 
FROM 
  (
    SELECT 
      anon_2.a_id AS anon_2_a_id, anon_2.a_parent_id AS anon_2_a_parent_id, anon_2.b_id AS anon_2_b_id,  anon_2.b_parent_id AS anon_2_b_parent_id 
    FROM 
      (
        SELECT 
          a.id AS a_id, a.parent_id AS a_parent_id, b.id AS b_id, b.parent_id AS b_parent_id 
        FROM a 
          LEFT OUTER JOIN b ON b.parent_id = a.parent_id 
        WHERE 
          a.parent_id = : parent_id_1 
        UNION 
        SELECT 
          a.id AS a_id, a.parent_id AS a_parent_id, b.id AS b_id, b.parent_id AS b_parent_id 
        FROM b 
          LEFT OUTER JOIN a ON a.parent_id = b.parent_id 
        WHERE 
          b.parent_id = : parent_id_2
      ) AS anon_2
  ) AS anon_1

```

This is the incorrect output using the commit referenced above included in 1.4.19
```sql
# AFTER, UNION
SELECT 
  anon_1.a_id AS anon_1_a_id,   anon_1.a_parent_id AS anon_1_a_parent_id,   anon_1.b_id AS anon_1_b_id,   anon_1.b_parent_id AS anon_1_b_parent_id 
FROM 
  (
    SELECT 
      a.id AS a_id, a.parent_id AS a_parent_id, b.id AS b_id, b.parent_id AS b_parent_id 
    FROM       a 
      LEFT OUTER JOIN b ON b.parent_id = a.parent_id 
    WHERE 
      a.parent_id = : parent_id_1 
    UNION 
    SELECT 
      a.id AS a_id, a.parent_id AS a_parent_id, b.id AS b_id, b.parent_id AS b_parent_id 
    FROM       b 
      LEFT OUTER JOIN a ON a.parent_id = b.parent_id 
    WHERE 
      b.parent_id = : parent_id_2
  ) AS anon_1 
  LEFT OUTER JOIN b ON anon_1.b_parent_id = anon_1.a_parent_id


# AFTER, UNION+COUNT
SELECT 
  count(*) AS count_1 
FROM 
  (
    SELECT 
      anon_2.a_id AS anon_2_a_id,       anon_2.a_parent_id AS anon_2_a_parent_id,       anon_2.b_id AS anon_2_b_id,       anon_2.b_parent_id AS anon_2_b_parent_id 
    FROM 
      (
        SELECT 
          a.id AS a_id, a.parent_id AS a_parent_id, b.id AS b_id, b.parent_id AS b_parent_id 
        FROM a 
          LEFT OUTER JOIN b ON b.parent_id = a.parent_id 
        WHERE 
          a.parent_id = : parent_id_1 
        UNION 
        SELECT 
          a.id AS a_id, a.parent_id AS a_parent_id, b.id AS b_id, b.parent_id AS b_parent_id 
        FROM b 
          LEFT OUTER JOIN a ON a.parent_id = b.parent_id 
        WHERE 
          b.parent_id = : parent_id_2
      ) AS anon_2 
      LEFT OUTER JOIN b ON anon_2.b_parent_id = anon_2.a_parent_id
  ) AS anon_1
```
